metadata.name: htop
metadata.description: Interactive process and system resource monitor

notes: htop is not included in standard Ubuntu installations
The package is available in Ubuntu's default repositories, so no additional repositories need to be added
installation.post_installation: After installation, simply run 'htop' to start the interactive monitor

overview.summary: htop is an interactive process viewer and system monitor that provides a real-time, colorful, and user-friendly interface for monitoring system resources (CPU, memory, swap) and managing processes. It's an enhanced alternative to the traditional 'top' command.
when_to_use: Monitor CPU and memory usage in real-time
View running processes with detailed information

syntax.description: htop runs as an interactive application without requiring file or process arguments in most cases.

misconceptions.title: htop requires root privileges to run
misconceptions.misconception: Many users think htop needs sudo to function
misconceptions.reality: htop can run as a regular user and show all processes. Root privileges are only needed for certain operations like renice to negative values or killing system processes.
misconceptions.tip: Run htop normally first. Only use sudo htop if you need to modify system processes.

misconceptions.title: htop shows all system information
misconceptions.misconception: htop displays everything about the system
misconceptions.reality: htop focuses on CPU, memory, and processes. For detailed system info, use other tools like df (disk space), iotop (I/O), or netstat (network).
misconceptions.tip: Use htop for CPU/memory/process monitoring. Combine with other tools for complete system monitoring.

misconceptions.title: High CPU percentage is always bad
misconceptions.misconception: If a process shows 100% CPU, something is wrong
misconceptions.reality: 100% CPU usage on one core is normal for single-threaded applications. Modern CPUs have multiple cores, so one process can't fully utilize all cores unless it's multi-threaded.
misconceptions.tip: Check if high CPU usage persists over time and if it affects system responsiveness before worrying.

misconceptions.title: htop and top are the same
misconceptions.misconception: htop is just a colorful version of top
misconceptions.reality: htop offers interactive controls (mouse support, better sorting, tree view), better visualization, and easier process management. However, top is more universally available and uses less resources.
misconceptions.tip: Use htop for interactive monitoring, top for scripts or minimal systems.

common_pitfalls.solution: Always verify the process name and PID before killing. Use F3 to search by name. Avoid killing processes you don't understand. System processes (owned by root) are usually safe to leave alone.

common_pitfalls.description: Setting very low delay values can cause htop itself to consume significant CPU
common_pitfalls.solution: Use default delay (1 second) for most cases. Only use faster updates (like -d 2) when necessary for short periods.

common_pitfalls.description: Colors may not display correctly in some terminal emulators
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -C flag for monochrome mode, or configure terminal color support. Check terminal color capabilities with echo $TERM

common_pitfalls.description: Some processes may be hidden or filtered out
common_pitfalls.solution: Press 'u' then select 'root' to see all processes including system ones. Check filters (F4) to ensure nothing is filtered.

best_practices: Use tree view (F5 or -t flag) to understand process relationships and find parent processes
Press F2 to customize the display - add/remove meters, change colors, and configure columns
Use F4 to filter processes when looking for specific applications
Sort by CPU% (F6) when troubleshooting performance issues
Sort by MEM% when checking for memory leaks
Use F9 to kill processes gracefully - try SIGTERM first, then SIGKILL if needed
Tag processes (Space) to perform batch operations on multiple processes
Monitor specific users (-u flag) when troubleshooting multi-user systems
performance_tips: htop itself uses minimal resources (~1-2% CPU) but setting very low delays increases overhead
Tree view adds slight overhead but provides valuable process relationship information
Filtering processes reduces CPU usage by showing fewer processes to update
On systems with many processes (1000+), consider filtering or using ps with grep for faster results

additional_notes.header_information: The header shows: CPU usage bars (per core), memory usage, swap usage, load average, uptime, and process/thread counts
additional_notes.process_information: Columns show: PID, user, priority (PR), nice value (NI), virtual memory (VIRT), resident memory (RES), shared memory (SHR), CPU%, MEM%, time running (TIME+), and command
additional_notes.color_coding: Process bars are color-coded: blue = low priority, green = normal, yellow = kernel threads, red = high priority
additional_notes.mouse_support: htop supports mouse interaction - click to select processes, scroll to navigate, click column headers to sort
additional_notes.configuration: User configuration is stored in ~/.config/htop/htoprc - settings persist between sessions
additional_notes.comparison_with_top: htop is more user-friendly but top is more universal and scriptable. Learn both for different use cases.
